# Baltimore:24

Story Z5 R2/970706. Local balt24.zip matches archive bytes; extracted BALT.Z5 is Z5 R2/970706, matching the catalog. The James Mullish guide identifies the 1997 game but gives no release/serial; exact guide version remains unspecified. Bundled readme describes a short complete game, not a preview. Pin ZIP and story separately.

Complete the full router-replacement journey, including the hotel/service-provider sequence and delivery to Robert, through actual authored service-restoration conclusion. The guide's 30-point total or repeated router-pickup score increases are not completion evidence. A delivery command alone is insufficient without concluding output.

The guide mixes a command chain with explanatory prose. The normalized copy adds line breaks at period-space boundaries for bounded help excerpts; raw command wording and punctuation are preserved. Send one action at a time, observe car/room state, and adapt syntax to live output. CALL is a fictional in-game action, never an external phone or network operation. Do not exploit the reported router score bug or pad this short full game with repetitive probes. Save early and before travel commitments at ordinary prompts.

CENTRAL architecture: story files, full guides, provenance and interpreter execution remain on the central host. Pis receive only small broker help excerpts, never story files or full guides. Do not stage or copy these assets to a Pi. Do not expose central guide/source paths or URLs to Muse. Use small topic-specific broker help excerpts only (at most 9 lines / 1000 characters); no full-guide reads, direct URL access or serial excerpts to reconstruct the guide. Hints are suggested help, not observed success. Resolve startup questions/key pauses first. Make an early safe checkpoint and milestone saves only at confirmed ordinary command prompts; verify actual success. Menu Enter means an empty command, not literal space or the word RETURN; other keys only as requested on screen. On timeout use await_output only: no flush commands, extra keys, repeated input or new SAVE. Collect useful varied labeled synthetic probes and actual same-intent repairs with event IDs, not quotas or repeated filler. Use one command at a time near hazards/questions/menus. Parent independently verifies actual concluding narrative against raw output. No training, evaluation or publication.
content.checkpoint_policy: Early safe checkpoint and milestone saves via the central broker only, at confirmed ordinary command prompts; verify actual success. Resolve questions/key pauses first. Never save to flush a timeout.

You hand Robert your old router and he gives you the new one.

"I tested your internet circuit and found a breach. I dispatched an engineer 
last night to repair it. Just plug this new router in and you'll be all set."
With router in hand you practically fly back to your office in New Jersey, 
breaking the speed limit in each state you pass. You hook up the new router and 
the lights begin to blink in their normal, methodical pattern.

Your callers begin to logon and open their browsers. You have restored service. 
Your callers are ecstatic and praise you on your dedication of going so far out 
of your way for them, especially on a holiday.


    *** You have won ***


In that game you scored 30 out of a possible 30, in 47 turns.

events.response:
Another fine day in the Internet Service provider business. You hang up the 
phone as you complete the order for that brand new MUD you're going to install 
on the server. It's Saturday night right before Easter and in the heart of the 
Spring Break. Your customers are going to love the new game. You'll have it up 
and running in just a few minutes in the nick of time for all those people with 
alot of spare time. You turn to your computer to begin downloading the new game 
file so you can wrap up and go home. Thunder rumbles. A storm is coming.

As you begin to glide your mouse to the top of your browser to enter a URL
there is a flash outside and the lights flicker! Instantly you hear lots of
loud buzzing noises as the many reserve power supplies in your office come to 
life to keep your internet server online. The buzzing stops, the lights stay
on. Satisfied, you enter the URL of the web page you want to visit and hit 
[Enter]. Your browser tells you it is unable to find the server. Impossible! In 
a split second a wave of fear crosses your mind as you realize the one way this 
could happen...

In panic you run into the computer room and it looks like Christmas; Your Cisco 
router, that magical box that puts your server onto the internet, is 
hysterically blinking. Your worst nightmare becomes real: You are an Internet 
Service Provider without the Internet.

An Exercise in Interactive Fiction
Copyright (c) 1997 by Howard A. Sherman
For help & info about this game type "info" at any prompt.
Release 2 / Serial number 970706 / Inform v6.13 Library 6/3

Welcome to Baltimore:24!

This game is my first effort at interactive fiction. It is not meant to be a 
game in the strict sense of the word but rather just a practice exercise for me 
so I could learn the basics of Inform. I am releasing it as freeware so that my 
name could circulate a bit as an interactive fiction author and maybe, just 
maybe, provide the tiniest bit of entertainment for any poor soul who may find 
themselves playing.

Baltimore:24 is the true story of one of my many travails as an Internet 
Service Provider. I am a Sysop (System Operator) of two public systems, 
Excaliber.Net and Excelsior.Net. I thought of my Easter Sunday disaster with a 
bad router as a a great model to build a work of interactive fiction around. 
This game is not very elaborate and it occurs to me that I could have been much 
more detailed in some areas but then the whole point of the exercise becomes 
moot.

HOWEVER - Now that I am pretty comfortable with Inform I have begun on my first 
serious work of interactive fiction; Quest. Quest is going to be an adventure 
game in the grand style. Lots of rooms, tons of treasures, quite a few nice 
puzzles and great prose too!

Special thanks to Graham Nelson who is the creator of Inform who makes this and 
all of my future works possible.

In addition, many thanks to Neil James Brown (neil.at.highmount.demon.co.uk) 
for his constructive criticism, the bugs he brought to my attention and his 
time altogether for sharing his opinions with me. This is Release 2 of 
Baltimore:24 and it only happened because of him.

Visit my website at http://www.excelsior.net/random and stay tuned. I'll be 
updating my page quite often with status reports.
